title: PAUL TOLD TIMOTHY TO DRINK WINE—BUT THE REASON MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING THE CHURCH HAS FORGOTTEN
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD TIMOTHY TO DRINK WINE—BUT THE REASON MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING THE CHURCH HAS FORGOTTEN
One sentence. One troubled stomach. One surprising instruction from an apostle. And a powerful lesson about holiness, healing, grace, and the God who cares for the body while transforming the soul.
“Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.” — 1 Timothy 5:23 (KJV)
Imagine spending your life trying to honor God.
You pray when nobody sees you. You resist temptations other people surrender to without a second thought. You study Scripture. You serve the church. You fight to keep your conscience clean.
And yet, your body keeps failing you.
You wake up tired. Your stomach hurts. Your strength disappears when you need it most. You ask God for healing, but tomorrow arrives with the same weakness.
Then a letter comes from someone who loves you deeply.
Someone who knows your faith.
Someone who has witnessed miracles, endured persecution, and encountered the risen Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul.
And instead of telling you to pray harder, fast longer, or prove your faith by enduring more pain, he writes something so ordinary that generations of Christians would eventually argue over it.
“Use a little wine.”
Wait.
Wine?
From Paul?
To Timothy?
In a letter containing serious instructions about holiness, church leadership, purity, and godly conduct?
Why would an apostle who warned believers against drunkenness recommend wine to a young pastor?
Was Paul permitting alcohol? Was he prescribing medicine? Was Timothy practicing complete abstinence? And what does any of this have to do with the Gospel?
The answer is more profound than the controversy.
Because hidden inside this easily misunderstood verse is a beautiful reminder that God never asked His children to confuse unnecessary suffering with spiritual maturity.
And to understand why, we must first meet the man receiving the instruction.
Timothy was not an ordinary young believer.
He was Paul's beloved coworker, a man shaped by sincere faith and entrusted with enormous responsibility.

His grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice had helped establish his spiritual foundation (2 Timothy 1:5). From childhood, he had known the sacred Scriptures that could make him wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ (2 Timothy 3:15).
Paul regarded him with extraordinary affection.
In 1 Timothy 1:2, he called him his own son in the faith.
Not because Timothy was Paul's biological child, but because their relationship had been formed through discipleship, spiritual responsibility, and shared devotion to Christ.
Timothy had witnessed the cost of following Jesus.
He knew that ministry was not a platform for applause.
It was a calling that demanded courage.
He had to confront false teaching, model godliness, care for believers, and lead faithfully in circumstances that could easily overwhelm a young minister.
And somewhere in the middle of those responsibilities, Timothy was frequently sick.
Scripture does not tell us exactly what illness he suffered from.
It does not identify an ulcer, infection, digestive disorder, or any other specific medical diagnosis.
What it does tell us is enough.
Timothy had stomach problems and recurring ailments.
And Paul knew about them.
That detail matters.
Because the apostle who cared about Timothy's doctrine also cared about Timothy's health.
The man who instructed him to guard the Gospel did not ignore the pain in his stomach.
Timothy was more than a worker in God's kingdom. He was a person worth caring for.
Now look closely at the original Greek.
Paul writes:
Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει, ἀλλὰ οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ χρῶ διὰ τὸν στόμαχον καὶ τὰς πυκνάς σου ἀσθενείας.
A careful translation is:
“No longer drink only water, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”
Several Greek expressions help us understand what Paul was actually saying.

The word ὑδροπότει (hydropotei) refers to drinking water. Combined with μηκέτι (mēketi), meaning “no longer,” the instruction indicates that Timothy should stop relying exclusively on water as his drink.
Paul was not commanding him to abandon water altogether.
The contrast is between drinking only water and making limited use of wine.
Then comes the phrase that should silence much of the careless debate.
οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ (oinō oligō).
“A little wine.”
The Greek word oinos ordinarily refers to wine, and oligos emphasizes a small quantity.
The text does not say, “Drink as much as you want.”
It does not say, “Use wine to escape your troubles.”
It does not say, “Your ministry is stressful, so intoxication is understandable.”
Paul's instruction is deliberately limited.
Then he gives the reason.
διὰ τὸν στόμαχον (dia ton stomachon).
“Because of your stomach.”
And finally:
τὰς πυκνάς σου ἀσθενείας (tas pyknas sou astheneias).
“Your frequent illnesses.”
The Greek adjective pyknas indicates recurring or frequent occurrences. Astheneias refers here to illnesses or bodily weaknesses.
Paul was addressing a real physical concern.
Not a social occasion.
Not an invitation to indulgence.
Not a new religious ritual.
A suffering believer needed practical care.
And the apostle gave him practical advice.
But here is where we must be especially careful.
Some Christians have claimed that the wine Paul recommended was definitely nonalcoholic grape juice.
Others have insisted that this verse proves every Christian should drink alcoholic beverages.
Neither conclusion follows from the text.
In ordinary first-century Greek usage, oinos could refer to fermented wine, and there is no clear indication in this verse that Paul meant unfermented juice.
At the same time, Paul's recommendation was specific to Timothy's condition and explicitly restricted to a little wine.
It was not a universal command requiring Christians to drink alcohol.
Nor does it establish that alcohol is a necessary or medically appropriate treatment for digestive illnesses today.
Modern medicine recognizes that alcohol can irritate the stomach, aggravate certain conditions, interact dangerously with medications, and contribute to serious health problems.
The ancient medical context must not be confused with present-day clinical advice.
Paul was speaking to Timothy in his historical circumstances, not writing a modern prescription for every believer with stomach pain.
That distinction protects us from forcing Scripture to say what it never intended to say.
But there is another question.
Why was Timothy apparently drinking only water?
Was he avoiding wine because of personal conviction?
Was he practicing unusually strict self-denial?
Was he concerned about his testimony?
Was he following an ascetic practice?
We are not told.
And faithful Bible interpretation requires the humility to admit what Scripture leaves unanswered.
It is possible that Timothy's abstinence reflected a personal discipline or concern for purity, but the passage does not explicitly reveal his motive.
What we know is that Paul considered a limited change appropriate for Timothy's health.
And that opens a much larger conversation.
Because sometimes believers begin to treat their own self-imposed restrictions as though they were commands from God.
They assume that if something is difficult, it must be holy.
If something is uncomfortable, it must be spiritually superior.
If they refuse every form of relief, perhaps God will be more pleased with them.
But Scripture never teaches that pain itself makes a person righteous.
Holiness is not measured by how much avoidable suffering we can accumulate.
And righteousness is not earned through the unnecessary neglect of our bodies.
Consider Paul's words in Colossians 2:23.

He warns about religious practices that possess an appearance of wisdom through self-imposed worship, false humility, and severe treatment of the body, yet lack genuine power against sinful indulgence.
That does not mean fasting is wrong.
It does not mean discipline is unnecessary.
Jesus Himself fasted.
Paul taught self-control.
The Christian life requires sacrifice.
But biblical self-denial is not the same as treating every physical need as an enemy of faith.
There is a difference between carrying the cross Christ calls us to carry and creating burdens Christ never commanded.
And perhaps someone reading this knows that difference all too painfully.
You have been exhausted for months.
But you keep telling yourself that rest is laziness.
You have been struggling emotionally.
But you feel ashamed to ask for help.
You have been sick.
But somewhere along the way, you began to believe that seeking treatment might reveal a lack of faith.
You love Jesus.
You truly do.
Yet you have started treating yourself with a harshness you would never impose upon someone you love.
Listen carefully.
Needing help does not make you less faithful.
Timothy was a devoted servant of Christ.
And Timothy was frequently ill.
Both statements were true at the same time.
His sickness did not erase his calling.
His weakness did not invalidate his faith.
His physical condition did not make him a spiritual failure.
And Paul's response was not condemnation.
It was care.
Think about that for a moment.
Paul had seen extraordinary works of God.
Acts 19:11–12 describes unusual miracles associated with his ministry, including healings.
Yet when addressing Timothy's recurring illnesses, Paul did not simply command him to demonstrate greater faith.
He offered practical counsel.
Why?
Scripture does not tell us why Timothy's illnesses persisted or why Paul chose this particular recommendation instead of describing a miraculous healing.
But the passage does show that practical measures and trust in God are not necessarily enemies.
We can pray for healing and seek appropriate medical care.
We can trust God's power while acknowledging our physical limitations.
We can believe in miracles without pretending every illness will disappear immediately.
Remember what Paul himself experienced.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–9, he described a painful affliction he called a thorn in the flesh.
He pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart.
And the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
We should not assume Paul's thorn was the same kind of illness Timothy experienced. Scripture does not identify it with certainty.
But the spiritual principle remains powerful.
God's grace does not depend upon the disappearance of every weakness.
Sometimes God delivers.
Sometimes He sustains.
Sometimes He works through ordinary means.
And sometimes, while we wait for answers, He reminds us that our value was never determined by our physical strength.
Now consider another detail that many people overlook.
Paul's advice appears in a letter that also warns against drunkenness.
In 1 Timothy 3:2–3, overseers are instructed to be temperate and not given to wine.
In 1 Timothy 3:8, deacons are warned against being devoted to much wine.
And in Ephesians 5:18, Paul writes:
There is no contradiction.
Paul could warn against drunkenness while recommending a small amount of wine for a particular physical problem.
The distinction is between limited use in a specific circumstance and the misuse of alcohol.
And that distinction matters because Christians sometimes approach Scripture looking for permission to do what they already want.
One person reads 1 Timothy 5:23 and announces, “See? The Bible says drinking is fine.”
Another reads the same verse and insists that Paul could not possibly have meant fermented wine.
But neither person's preferences should determine the meaning of Scripture.
We must allow the Word of God to correct us rather than forcing it to confirm us.
Proverbs 20:1 warns about wine's power to deceive.
Proverbs 23:29–35 vividly portrays the suffering associated with excessive drinking.
Romans 14 teaches believers to consider the consciences and spiritual welfare of others.
And 1 Corinthians 6:12 reminds us that even when something may be permissible, we must not allow ourselves to be mastered by it.
Therefore, 1 Timothy 5:23 cannot reasonably be used to defend drunkenness, addiction, reckless drinking, or disregard for another person's spiritual vulnerability.
Nor should it be used to shame Christians who choose complete abstinence.
Some believers abstain because of conscience.
Some because of family history.
Some because of addiction recovery.
Some because of health concerns or medications.
Some because they believe abstinence best serves their witness and responsibilities.
Such decisions deserve serious respect.
And anyone who struggles with alcohol dependence should never feel pressured to drink because Paul gave Timothy this instruction.
Christian freedom is never a command to become enslaved.
But there is an even deeper lesson here.
One that reaches far beyond wine.
What kind of God do we imagine when we think about holiness?
A God who watches us suffer and demands that we prove our devotion by refusing help?
Or the God revealed in Jesus Christ, who calls sinners to repentance, confronts destructive behavior, and also shows extraordinary compassion toward human weakness?
Look at Jesus.
When He encountered the sick, He did not treat their suffering as an inconvenience.
When a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years approached Him, He received her with compassion and restored her (Mark 5:25–34).
When a blind man cried out for mercy, Jesus did not silence him. He responded to his need (Mark 10:46–52).
When the crowds were hungry, Jesus cared about their physical condition (Mark 8:1–9).
And when His disciples returned from demanding ministry, He told them:
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.” — Mark 6:31 (KJV)
Rest.
From Jesus.
To people serving Him.
How many believers need to hear those words today?
You can love God deeply and still need sleep.
You can serve faithfully and still need nourishment.
You can be spiritually mature and still need medical attention.
You can be filled with the Holy Spirit and still experience physical weakness.
Your body is not an obstacle to your salvation.
It is part of your created humanity, and God calls you to honor Him with it.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 teaches believers that their bodies belong to God and that they are to glorify Him in their bodies.
The immediate context concerns sexual immorality, so we should not pretend Paul was specifically discussing diet, medicine, or alcohol in those verses.
Nevertheless, the passage reminds us that our physical lives matter to the Lord.
Our bodies are not disposable instruments for religious productivity.
They are part of the lives we have been entrusted to steward.
And this brings us to something deeply personal.
There are Christians who have spent years serving everyone except themselves.
They visit the sick while ignoring their own symptoms.
They comfort the grieving while refusing to acknowledge their own sorrow.
They pray for struggling families while silently watching their own relationships deteriorate.
They encourage others to seek help while believing they must handle everything alone.
And eventually, something gives way.
Sometimes it is their health.
Sometimes it is their emotional endurance.
Sometimes it is their ability to keep serving with joy.
They are not necessarily rebellious.
They may simply be exhausted.
And perhaps the most compassionate thing they need to hear is not another demand to do more.
Perhaps they need to remember that even Timothy, a trusted minister of the Gospel, received permission to address a physical problem.
Paul did not tell Timothy to abandon his calling.
He told him to care for his stomach.
There is something beautifully human about that.
The Christian life is not an endless performance of invincibility.
We follow a Savior who entered human history in real flesh.
Jesus knew hunger.
He knew thirst.
He knew exhaustion.
John 4:6 describes Him sitting by Jacob's well, wearied from His journey.
John 19:28 records Him saying, “I thirst,” during His crucifixion.
And Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our great High Priest can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Jesus is not distant from the reality of human frailty.
He understands what it means to inhabit a vulnerable human body.
But His mission went infinitely beyond showing sympathy.
He came to save sinners.
That is where this entire conversation must ultimately lead.
Because our deepest problem is not merely that our bodies become sick.
It is that our hearts are corrupted by sin.
We can receive excellent medical treatment and still remain spiritually lost.
We can practice perfect self-discipline and still be separated from God.
We can avoid alcohol, maintain strict religious habits, and appear respectable before others while secretly carrying pride, bitterness, lust, dishonesty, unforgiveness, or unbelief.
Outward discipline cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
And physical health cannot reconcile a sinner to a holy God.
Only Jesus Christ can do that.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
But the story does not end with our guilt.
Romans 5:8 announces:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
This is the Gospel.
Not that we made ourselves acceptable through perfect performance.
Not that we earned forgiveness by suffering enough.
Not that we became righteous through strict religious routines.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore our sins, died upon the cross, and rose again.
He did what we could never do.
He accomplished what our discipline could never achieve.
And He offers forgiveness and reconciliation to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
But God's undeserved favor that saves us and teaches us to live transformed lives.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine holiness possible.
And this is why the theme of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply.
Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
The scandal is not merely what other people discovered about your past.
It is what God already knows about every human heart.
The hidden sins.
The excuses.
The failures.
The compromises.
The years spent trying to appear spiritually healthy while remaining inwardly wounded by guilt.
Yet the grace of Jesus Christ reaches people who cannot rescue themselves.
He does not excuse their sin.
He calls them to turn from it.
He does not leave them imprisoned in shame.
He offers forgiveness.
He does not promise that following Him will remove every earthly hardship.
He promises that those who belong to Him will never be abandoned.
And His resurrection assures us that suffering, sin, and death will not have the final word.
Perhaps your scandal was public.
Perhaps nobody knows what happened.
Perhaps you have been living with the consequences of a decision you wish you could undo.
Or perhaps your struggle is quieter.
You have become so committed to appearing strong that you no longer know how to admit you are weak.
You can explain theology to others.
But you struggle to believe that God's mercy still reaches you.
You can quote verses about grace.
But you punish yourself for failures Christ calls you to bring into the light.
Listen.
Repentance is necessary.
Confession matters.
Obedience matters.
But self-punishment cannot accomplish what Christ's sacrifice has already accomplished.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
You do not need to pretend your sin was harmless.
You need to bring it honestly before the Savior.
You do not need to manufacture your own righteousness.
You need the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ.
And you do not need to prove that you are spiritually strong enough to deserve God's attention.
You need to come to Him in humility.
Even with your weakness.
Even with your trembling faith.
Even with the questions you have been afraid to ask.
Now return to that small instruction in 1 Timothy 5:23.
“Use a little wine.”
It is easy to become so distracted by the word wine that we miss the tenderness of the moment.
An apostle was concerned about a younger minister's recurring illness.
The letter was filled with matters of enormous spiritual significance.
False teachers had to be confronted.
The church needed order.
Leaders needed integrity.
The Gospel had to be guarded.
Yet Paul's attention did not become so consumed with the mission that he forgot the person carrying it.
He remembered Timothy's stomach.
He remembered his frequent illnesses.
He cared enough to say something practical.
That should challenge the way we practice discipleship.
Do we only ask people how their ministry is going?
Or do we ask how they are actually doing?
Do we celebrate their service while overlooking their suffering?
Do we admire their strength while making it impossible for them to admit weakness?
Do we encourage prayer while also helping people access appropriate care?
A healthy Christian community should be a place where truth is proclaimed, sin is confronted, grace is extended, and suffering people are not treated as failures.
James 5:14–16 calls the church to pray for the sick.
Galatians 6:2 calls believers to bear one another's burdens.
And Romans 12:15 tells us to weep with those who weep.
The church is not supposed to be a gathering of people pretending they never struggle.
It is a redeemed family learning to follow Christ together.
Some need correction.
Some need encouragement.
Some need rest.
Some need medical care.
Some need help escaping destructive habits.
Some need to hear the Gospel clearly for the first time.
And all of us need Jesus.
That is why this passage should never become merely an argument about whether Christians may drink wine.
The question is important, and Scripture deserves careful interpretation.
But the verse also teaches us to distinguish God's actual commands from human assumptions.
It teaches us to value truth over convenience.
It teaches us that practical care can coexist with deep faith.
And it reminds us that Christian maturity is not demonstrated by pretending we have no limitations.
Maybe you have spent years trying to impress God with your strength.
But what if today you finally stopped pretending?
What if you confessed the sin you have been hiding?
What if you sought help for the suffering you have been minimizing?
What if you stopped using religious activity to avoid confronting what is happening inside your heart?
What if you discovered that surrender is not the end of your story, but the beginning of a transformed life in Christ?
Jesus said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
Notice whom He invited.
The weary.
The burdened.
The people who could no longer carry everything themselves.
And His invitation still stands.
Not as a promise that every problem will disappear overnight.
But as a call to come under His gracious lordship and find rest for the soul.
If this article has touched a struggle you rarely speak about, you do not have to tell the whole world your private story.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Someone reading may desperately need to know they are not alone.
Your honesty may encourage a believer who has been suffering in silence.
And your testimony may direct someone toward the Savior who sustained you.
If a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them gently, or sending this article to them privately.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to diagnose their spiritual condition.
But to remind them that their worth is not measured by how successfully they hide their pain.
Your family may read it.
A friend who has stopped attending church may encounter it.
Someone quietly wrestling with guilt may discover a reminder of Christ's mercy.
Even a person who does not yet believe may begin asking serious questions about Jesus.
You cannot control what another person does with the message.
But you can faithfully help make it available.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because the Scripture behind it deserves to be revisited.
Come back to 1 Timothy 5:23 when you are tempted to confuse unnecessary suffering with holiness.
Come back to 2 Corinthians 12:9 when weakness makes you feel ashamed.
Come back to Matthew 11:28 when your soul is exhausted.
And come back to the cross when your conscience reminds you of sins you cannot undo.
Our desire is to keep opening the Scriptures, confronting difficult questions, encouraging repentance, and pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
Not merely toward emotional inspiration that fades by tomorrow.
But toward truth that forms disciples.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical knowledge, prayer, spiritual maturity, and faithful Christian living.
But keeping Gospel-centered resources available and continuing to develop new teaching takes time, work, and financial support.
That is why I want to extend a personal invitation.
For believers who choose to make this part of their regular Christian giving, it can be an expression of generosity toward Gospel ministry, much like other voluntary offerings.
But it is important to be biblically clear.
Christians glorify God through faith, obedience, love, generosity, service, and lives surrendered to Him.

Scripture encourages believers to support worthwhile Gospel work (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; Philippians 4:15–17), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing rather than compelled.
I will not suggest that a monthly payment purchases divine favor.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Think of the people who may encounter a Scripture explanation because someone helped make it possible.
Think of the believer searching for encouragement late at night.
The parent looking for a devotional.
The young Christian trying to understand a difficult Bible passage.
The person who has wandered from church and is cautiously beginning to seek God again.
We cannot promise how many lives will be changed.
Only God knows the full fruit of faithful ministry.
But we can work together to keep sharing the truth.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal encouragement, or meaningful gifts for others.
It is not the reason anyone must give.
The greater purpose is to support the continuing work of sharing Scripture, strengthening disciples, and proclaiming Jesus Christ.
Now, before you leave, remember Timothy.
A faithful servant.
A young minister.
A man carrying serious responsibilities.
A believer whose body was not always cooperating with his calling.
And Paul, the great apostle, took time to care about something as ordinary as his stomach.
It is almost startling how much tenderness can fit inside one verse.
Maybe that is what someone needed to see today.
God is not honored by our prideful refusal to acknowledge that we are human.
He is honored when we trust Him enough to obey His Word, acknowledge our need, receive appropriate help, and walk faithfully in the strength He provides.
The Gospel does not promise a life without weakness.
It promises a Savior whose grace is sufficient.
It does not promise that faithful Christians will never suffer.
It reveals a risen Lord who will one day make all things new.
And it does not teach that the strongest believer is the one who never needs help.
It teaches us to depend upon Jesus Christ.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Ask for help where you are struggling.
Care for the body God has entrusted to you.
Love the people He has placed around you.
And never allow an argument about one small cup of wine to distract you from the immeasurably greater gift of salvation through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Because the most important thing Paul offered Timothy was not advice about a beverage.
It was a life devoted to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And the most important thing you can receive today is not a temporary remedy for an earthly problem.
It is the grace of the Savior who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
You may be carrying a weakness that has not disappeared, but you do not have to carry your life without the Savior who knows your name, sees your suffering, and calls you to Himself.
